title: How Rising U.S. Health Insurance Costs Affect Your Savings Targets
description: Adjusting your FIRE number and monthly budget for medical inflation.
content:
Medical inflation consistently outpaces general inflation in the US. While CPI might be 3%, healthcare costs often rise 6-8% annually. This creates a 'silent leak' in long-term financial plans. If you are saving for retirement based on today's insurance premiums, you are likely underfunding your future. Understanding the trajectory of premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket maximums is mandatory for anyone planning to retire before Medicare age (65).

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Gap' Years: If you retire at 55, you have 10 years before Medicare. You must self-fund insurance via the ACA (Obamacare). Budget $1,000-$2,000/month for this.
  • HSA as Defense: A fully funded Health Savings Account is your best hedge. It grows tax-free to pay for future inflated bills.
  • Inflation Adjustment: When calculating your 'Financial Independence Number', add a 10-15% buffer specifically for healthcare. $2.5M might actually need to be $2.8M.
  • Subsidy Management: In early retirement, keeping your taxable income low (by living off cash/Roth) can qualify you for massive ACA subsidies, saving $15k/year.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US system is unique in that healthcare is an asset-protection issue. One major illness without proper coverage can drain a retirement account. You are managing 'Longevity Risk' and 'Morbidity Risk' simultaneously.

The Cost Projection

Projecting the undefeatable curve of medical costs.

Premiums vs. Usage

You pay twice: once to have the insurance (Premium) and once to use it (Deductible/Copay).

  • Current Trend: Deductibles are rising fast. A 'Bronze' plan might have a $7,000 deductible. You need that cash liquid.
  • Premium Inflation: Expect premiums to double every 10-12 years. If it costs $600/mo now, budget $1,200/mo for your future self.

The Retiree Estimate

Fidelity estimates a couple retiring today needs $315,000 (after tax) just for medical expenses. This does not include Long Term Care (nursing homes).

Long Term Care (LTC)

Nursing homes cost $100k/year. Medicare does not pay for this. Medicaid only pays if you are broke. Self-insuring or buying LTC insurance is the only bridge.

Defensive Saving Tactics

  1. Max the HSA Today: Treat it as a 401(k). Invest it in stocks. Do not touch it for current bills if possible. Let it grow for 20 years to cover the $315k gap.
  2. LTC Sinking Fund: Start a specific brokerage account for 'Late Life Care'. Put $200/mo in it. It's cheaper than insurance and stays yours if you don't need it.
  3. Health Maintenance: The best financial move is staying healthy. Diet and exercise reduce your lifetime risk of diabetes and heart disease, the most expensive conditions.
  4. ACA Subsidy Planning: Learn how MAGI (Modified Adjusted Gross Income) determines subsidies. Plan your withdrawals to keep income low in years 55-65.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Medicare cover everything?

No. It covers ~80%. You still pay premiums (Part B), deductibles, and drug costs (Part D). And no dental/vision/hearing usually.

Should I move abroad?

Medical tourism or retiring abroad (Portugal/Costa Rica) is a valid financial strategy. Healthcare costs can be 70% lower. But verify insurance eligibility as an expat.

Is critical illness insurance worth it?

Maybe. It pays a lump sum if you get cancer/heart attack. If you have a family history, it's a reasonable hedge.
